title: Galba, Otho and the Rhine armies
sum: Tacitus begins in January of the year Galba was consul for the second time and tells why he writes: after Actium honest history faded, and he will speak of every man without love or hate (1:1). He lists the disasters of the age (1:2), says the gods seemed to care only to punish (1:3), and then goes back to survey Rome, the armies and the provinces when Nero died (1:4-11).

From 1:12 the year unfolds in order. The legions on the Rhine refuse their oath. Galba, old and unpopular with the unpaid soldiers, adopts Piso on 10 January. Five days later Otho, who has been courting the Guard, is hailed emperor, and Galba and Piso are killed that same day. The Senate rushes to flatter him (1:12-49). Then the Rhine armies hail Vitellius and march on Italy by two roads, Otho prepares for war and Rome is shaken by a night riot, omens and a flood (1:50-90). The book ends on 14 March with Otho leaving Rome.
readings: A senator writing about thirty years after the events puts the civil war in order: a day-by-day account of Galba's fall in January and Rome's mood in the weeks after, then the German armies' rise, with the reasons beneath each turn (1:4).

The same empire is the world of Luke 2:1, Luke 3:1, Acts and the letters. Tacitus names the army, the Guard, the Senate, procurators, citizenship and the emperor's household, all things the New Testament mentions in passing. His verdict that the gods only punish (1:3) is the clearest place where the Bible answers him.
Read as a study of flattery and power
The book keeps returning to flattery: of emperors (1:1), by senators to Otho (1:45), and by crowds (1:90). Proverbs says a smooth tongue is a net (Proverbs 29:5).

views.C: A Christian reads Book 1 as an honest outsider's picture of the empire that Jesus was born under and the apostles worked in. Where it overlaps the Bible, it agrees on the facts (emperors, Guard, citizenship, famine, signs from the sky) and differs on what they mean: Tacitus says "the gods care nothing for our safety, only for punishing us" (1:3), while Jesus says not one sparrow falls without the Father (Matthew 10:29-31) and God says, "I take no pleasure in the death of a wicked man" (Ezekiel 33:11). The Bible tells Christians to pray for those in power (1 Timothy 2:1-2) and to honor the king (1 Peter 2:17), even for such rulers. The war in Judea first appears at 1:10; many Christians read Jesus' words about Jerusalem encircled by armies (Luke 21:20-24) of its fall in AD 70.
views.H: Book 1 can be set beside Suetonius, Plutarch and Josephus, who tell some of the same events. They agree on the main events and differ on details: 23 or 15 conspirators, the astrologer's name, Galba's last words and his killer (see the notes at 1:22, 1:27 and 1:41). Tacitus names Cluvius Rufus as a governor (1:8), and Wikipedia lists him among the authorities Tacitus cites. His speeches are his own writing, and he says a speech may have been written by someone else (1:90). Wikipedia's page on Domitian cites the historian Brian Jones, who says the bias of the surviving sources makes Domitian hard to judge, and its page on Tacitus says Domitian's reign left him "jaded and perhaps ashamed at his own complicity." A reader should hold that beside Tacitus's promise of fairness (1:1).
views.R: For the first readers, a Roman year was named by two consuls (1:1), soldiers swore a personal oath to the emperor (1:55), the Guard expected a bonus (1:5), and Knights, freedmen and senators had fixed places (1:4, 1:13). Omens came from storms, birds and the liver (1:18, 1:27, 1:62). They knew the Forum, the Capitol and the Lake of Curtius (1:2, 1:41), and the date forms of Kalends, Nones and Ides (1:18, 1:27, 1:57, 1:90).
views.J: Josephus tells Galba, Otho and Vitellius in a few lines and says he omits the rest because the story is well known (Jewish War 4.9.2). He says Vespasian put off the war against Jerusalem and waited, that Titus turned back when he heard Galba was dead, and that Galba reigned seven months and as many days. Tacitus has Vespasian send Titus to Galba (1:10) and the army of Judea swear Otho's oath (1:76); he tells Titus's turning back in Book 2, with a different reason (2:1-2), and gives no length for Galba's reign. Acts and the Gospels name Augustus, Tiberius and Claudius, and use "Caesar" for the emperor; Tiberius Alexander appears in Josephus with the sons of Judas the Galilean named in Acts 5:37; Agrippa II sailed with Titus (Josephus) and is the king who heard Paul (Acts 25:13). Philippians has "the whole praetorium" and "Caesar's household." Revelation 17:10's seven kings are counted in the site's note on that verse.

deep.b:
Book 1 covers 1 January to 14 March AD 69.

  • 9 June 68: Nero dies (Wikipedia).
  • 1 to 3 January: the Rhine legions refuse their oath and hail Vitellius (1:55-57).
  • 10 January: Galba adopts Piso, in a storm (1:18).
  • 15 January: Otho is hailed at the golden milestone, Galba and Piso are killed, the Senate votes Otho every honor (1:27-47).
  • January to March (Tacitus gives no dates): Vitellius's armies move by two roads under Valens and Caecina (1:61-70); Otho keeps Marius Celsus and hears of the provinces' choices (1:71-76).
  • Before 14 March (Tacitus gives no date for the riot): the night riot, omens and the flood (1:80-86); on 14 March Otho leaves Rome (1:90).

Full list in the notes; the main points:

  • Emperors: Augustus (1:15; Luke 2:1), Tiberius (1:15; Luke 3:1), Claudius (1:16; Acts 11:28; Acts 18:2), Nero as "Caesar" (1:5; Acts 25:11-12).
  • People: Pompey (1:15), Tiberius Alexander (1:11; Acts 5:37 through Josephus), Agrippa II (1:10 through Josephus; Acts 25:13), Poppaea (1:13 through Josephus), Vespasian and Titus (1:1, 1:10).
  • Offices: the Praetorian Guard (1:5, 1:13; Philippians 1:13), Roman Knights (1:4), procurators (1:7, 1:11, 1:12; Acts 23:24; Acts 25:11-12), centurions (1:83; Luke 7:8; Acts 10:1), citizenship (1:8, 1:78; Acts 22:28).
  • Places: Judea (1:10, 1:76), Syria (1:10; Luke 2:2), Egypt and Alexandria (1:11, 1:31; Acts 27:6; Acts 18:24), Illyricum (1:9; Romans 15:19), Cappadocia (1:78; Acts 2:9), Philippi (1:50; Acts 16:12), Achaia (1:23; Acts 18:12), Spain (1:8; Romans 15:24), Dalmatia (1:76; 2 Timothy 4:10), the Parthians (1:2, 1:40; Acts 2:9).
  • Practices: reading the liver (1:27; Ezekiel 21:21), astrologers (1:22; Isaiah 47:13), tribute (1:8; Matthew 22:17), the soldiers' bonus and fees (1:5, 1:46; Luke 3:14), famine (1:73; Acts 11:28), signs from the sky (1:3, 1:86; Luke 21:11; the speaking ox and Numbers 22:28), the emperor's image (1:41; Matthew 22:20).

deep.h: Where the ancient writers agree and differ
deep.b:
• Agree: Galba's death near the Lake of Curtius (Suetonius, Plutarch); the storm at the adoption (Plutarch); the builders' signal to Otho (Suetonius, Plutarch); Galba's question to the soldier who claimed to have killed Otho (all three); the tribune Martialis (Plutarch); Densus's defence (Plutarch); Galba's reign of seven months and seven days (Josephus; Suetonius says the seventh month).
  • Differ: the number who first hailed Otho (23 in Tacitus and Plutarch; fifteen conspirators in Suetonius); the astrologer's name (Ptolemaeus in Tacitus; Seleucus in Suetonius); Galba's last words; who struck the blow (Tacitus: Terentius, Laecanius or Camurius; Plutarch: Camurius by most writers' account); where Galba's head was found.

deep.title: Why Josephus leaves out what Tacitus tells
deep.b: My theory: Josephus says the civil wars are "well known by all" and described by many Greek and Roman writers, so he "touched upon" them only for connection (Jewish War 4.9.2). For his readers the part that mattered was the pause in Judea: Vespasian "stood waiting whither the empire would be transferred." Tacitus tells what was happening at Rome and on the Rhine in those same weeks. In Book 1 the East "hadn't moved yet" (1:10), and the army of Judea swore Otho's oath (1:76). Read together, Rome's civil war is the delay in Jerusalem's siege. This is my reading of how they fit, not a claim that either used the other. A web search on 3 November 2026 found no published account that sets the two books side by side this way.

echoes: Luke 2:1; Luke 3:1; Luke 3:14; Luke 7:8; Luke 21:9-11; Luke 21:20-24; Matthew 10:29-31; Matthew 22:17-21; Matthew 24:6-7; Acts 5:37; Acts 11:28; Acts 18:2; Acts 22:25-28; Acts 25:11-13; Acts 28:16; Acts 28:31; Philippians 1:13; Philippians 4:22; Romans 13:1-7; 1 Timothy 2:1-2; 1 Peter 2:13-17; Revelation 13:3; Revelation 17:10; Ezekiel 21:21; Isaiah 47:13; Deuteronomy 18:10-12; Acts 10:1; Romans 15:24; Numbers 22:28; 2 Timothy 4:10

settings.what: The preface
settings.by: Tacitus, speaking as the author
settings.to: his Roman readers, senators and other educated Romans
settings.when: when he opens the Histories, more than thirty years after the year it covers
settings.why: To say why the book is written and how it will be told: from the year Galba was consul for the second time, with truth promised even though the writer owes his rank to the Flavian emperors. It also names the age he wants to write about in his old age, the time of Nerva and Trajan. Knowing the readers lived under the Flavians and Nerva makes the praise of free speech more pointed.
settings.readers: Roman readers in the years after Domitian's death. Wikipedia's list of Tacitus's works dates the Histories to 105 (a bare entry in the list), and Tacitus was a senator by then; the text speaks as one Roman to others ("our city," 1:22; "we," 1:18). The preface tells them he owes his rank to the Flavian emperors and still promises fairness (1:1).
views: The author's claim
He owes Galba, Otho and Vitellius nothing and will write without love or hate (1:1).
A historian's caution

Wikipedia says Domitian's reign left Tacitus "jaded and perhaps ashamed at his own complicity," and cites the historian Brian Jones, who says the bias of the surviving sources makes Domitian hard to judge.

settings.what: A letter from Pompeius Propinquus
settings.by: the procurator of Belgica, Pompeius Propinquus
settings.to: Galba in Rome
settings.when: a few days after 1 January 69
settings.why: To tell Galba that the legions of Upper Germany had broken their oath, wanted another emperor and would leave the choice to the Senate and people. It hurried Galba's plan to adopt an heir. The sender was killed within days (1:58).
settings.readers: Readers who knew how the year ended see a warning that reached Galba in time and did not save him. Tacitus tells the death of the man who sent it at 1:58.

settings.what: Galba's speech adopting Piso
settings.by: Galba, as Tacitus reports it ("they say")
settings.to: Piso Licinianus, with Vinius, Laco, Marius Celsus and Ducenius Geminus present (1:14)
settings.when: 10 January 69, before the announcement to the camp
settings.why: To give the reasons for choosing Piso, to warn him that success is a harder test than misery, and to defend adoption as the way to find the best ruler now that the family of the Julii and Claudii was over. The speech is also Tacitus's own reflection on empire, put in Galba's mouth.
settings.readers: Readers who knew that Piso lasted only days (1:48) hear Galba praise adoption as the way to find the best ruler (1:16). The "they say" (1:15) tells them the words are Tacitus's version.
views: As Tacitus gives it
A long, measured address (1:15-16), after which Galba spoke "as if he were making an emperor."
Plutarch
Plutarch has Galba go to the camp to name Piso, and says thunder, lightning and rain broke into the reading of his address (Galba 23).

settings.what: Galba announces the adoption to the soldiers
settings.by: Galba
settings.to: the assembled soldiers at the Praetorian camp
settings.when: 10 January 69, in a storm
settings.why: To tell the Guard he had adopted Piso "as soldiers do when one picks a comrade," and that the mutinous 4th and 22nd legions on the Rhine would soon be back in line. He offered no gift, and Tacitus says a small one would have won them.
settings.readers: Readers who had met the Guard's grievance at 1:5 see that Galba gave no gift and spoke "as briefly as an emperor does." Tacitus tells them a small gift could have won the men.

settings.what: Galba and Piso address the Senate
settings.by: Galba, then Piso
settings.to: the senators
settings.when: 10 January 69 or the days just after
settings.why: To present the adoption to the Senate for its approval. Galba spoke no better than he had to the soldiers; Piso spoke graciously and the senators backed him.
settings.readers: The senators among Tacitus's readers knew what a hearing before the Senate meant. Here the senators back the adoption, and at 1:45-47 they vote every honor to Otho.

settings.what: Piso's speech to the cohort on guard at the Palace
settings.by: Piso Licinianus
settings.to: the cohort on duty at the Palace, in front of the steps
settings.when: 15 January 69, the "sixth day" since his adoption, while Otho was being carried to the camp
settings.why: To keep the cohort loyal by contrasting himself with Otho, whom he charged with luxury and with owing the empire to vice, and to remind the soldiers that their honor was unbroken and a bonus for loyalty would come from Galba and himself. The bodyguards drifted away as he spoke, and the rest of the cohort took up their standards (1:31).
settings.readers: Readers who know that Piso is killed within hours (1:43) read a calm speech that Tacitus lets fail. He says the bodyguards drifted away as Piso spoke and the rest of the cohort took up their standards (1:31).
views: Tacitus
Piso is calm and modest; the speech is stern against Otho (1:29-30).
Plutarch and Suetonius
Neither gives the speech. Plutarch has Piso sent ahead to the camp (Galba 26-27); Suetonius has Otho send killers for Galba and Piso (Otho 6.3).

settings.what: The advisers' debate
settings.by: Titus Vinius, and the others (with Laco speaking against Vinius)
settings.to: Galba, in the Palace
settings.when: 15 January 69, as the news of Otho reached the Palace
settings.why: To advise Galba whether to stay in the Palace and hold it, or to go out and meet the rising. Vinius argued for waiting and holding the doors; the others argued for acting before the plot grew. Galba chose to go out (1:34).
settings.readers: Readers know that Galba went out and died (1:41), so the debate shows who pushed him toward the Forum. Tacitus has Vinius for staying and Laco attacking Vinius.

settings.what: Otho's speech to the soldiers
settings.by: Otho, newly hailed emperor
settings.to: the Praetorian soldiers and the legion from the fleet, at the camp's rampart
settings.when: 15 January 69, after the soldiers had put him on Galba's platform
settings.why: To turn a mob that had made him emperor into an army that would march on the Forum: he listed Galba's killings and Icelus's and Vinius's greed, claimed the gods had turned from the adoption, and said the weapons of every soldier were on his side. Then he had the armory opened.
settings.readers: Readers who already know the facts behind the names on Otho's list (1:5-7, 1:37) can judge it as a politician's list. Tacitus lets the speech stand beside his own account.
views: Tacitus's report
A speech built from the killings Galba ordered and the bonus never paid.
Caution
Otho's list is a politician's list; see the notes at 1:37 on each name.

settings.what: Galba's last words
settings.by: Galba, in the Forum
settings.to: the men attacking him
settings.when: 15 January 69, near the Lake of Curtius
settings.why: Tacitus gives two versions of what Galba said: a plea for a few days to pay the bonus, or an offer of his throat "if that seemed best for the state." He says it made no difference to those killing him.
settings.readers: Readers get the scene of Galba's death in the Forum, a place they knew, with Tacitus's plain statement that the reports of his words differ.
views: Tacitus
Reports differ "depending on whether people hated him or admired him."
Suetonius
Gives a cry to the soldiers that he was theirs and they his, and the report of the offered neck (Galba 20.1).
Plutarch
Galba offers his neck and says, "Do your work, if this is better for the Roman people" in sense (Galba 27.1).

settings.what: Valens pushes Vitellius to claim the throne
settings.by: Fabius Valens, legate of a legion
settings.to: Aulus Vitellius, commander of the Lower army
settings.when: before the mutiny, at a time Tacitus does not give
settings.why: To spur a slow man to take the empire: he pointed to the soldiers' fire, Britain and the German auxiliaries, the old man's rule on loan, and Vitellius's father's three consulships. The speech is reported, not quoted.
settings.readers: Readers who know how the year ended see the push that turned a slow man into a claimant. Tacitus reports the speech and does not quote it.

settings.what: The Lingones' envoys to the legions
settings.by: envoys of the Lingones, in rags and sorrow
settings.to: the legions in the camps
settings.when: in the winter before the 1 January oath
settings.why: To stir the legions against Galba by complaining of their people's injuries and neighbors' rewards. The legions came close to mutiny before Hordeonius Flaccus sent the envoys away at night (1:54).
settings.readers: Readers were told at 1:8 that the Gallic states nearest the German armies had been denied the honors Galba gave others, so the envoys' complaint is the grievance Tacitus already set out.

settings.what: Lugdunum urges the soldiers against Vienna
settings.by: the people of Lugdunum
settings.to: Fabius Valens's soldiers on the march
settings.when: early 69, while Valens's army was on the march
settings.why: To pay back an old quarrel by pointing the army at Vienna, with talk of plunder and of a city that had backed Vindex and Galba. Vienna's people begged for mercy and were fined (1:66).
settings.readers: Readers meet an old quarrel between two Gallic cities that Tacitus says was too bitter to be only about Nero and Galba (1:65).

settings.what: Fabius Valens urges the army to spare Vienna
settings.by: Fabius Valens
settings.to: his soldiers on the march, after the people of Vienna begged for mercy
settings.when: early in 69, as Valens's army passed Vienna on the way to the Alps
settings.why: To turn the army from destroying Vienna after Lugdunum had pushed it to plunder the city. Tacitus says the age and rank of the colony counted for something and Valens's words were heard fairly; the city was fined its arms and helped the soldiers with supplies. He adds a steady report that Valens had been bought for a large sum.
settings.readers: Readers see the man who pushed Vitellius to revolt (1:52) speaking for mercy, with Tacitus's note that he was said to have been bought, so they weigh the speech with that report beside it.

settings.what: Claudius Cossus's plea for the Helvetii
settings.by: Claudius Cossus, an envoy of the Helvetii
settings.to: Vitellius and the soldiers
settings.when: early 69, after Caecina's war
settings.why: To win pardon for a defeated state. Tacitus says he hid his skill in speaking behind a fitting show of fear, and that the soldiers burst into tears and granted pardon and safety.
settings.readers: Readers see a defeated people plead before soldiers, and Tacitus notes that the envoy hid his skill at speaking behind a fitting show of fear.

settings.what: Otho receives Marius Celsus
settings.by: Otho, then Marius Celsus, who admits the charge
settings.to: Marius Celsus, the consul-elect, summoned to the Capitol
settings.when: in the weeks after the coup, while Vitellius's armies gathered; Tacitus gives no date
settings.why: To win a name for mercy from a distinguished man on the other side. Celsus admitted staying faithful to Galba and claimed the example as a credit. Otho called the gods to witness their reconciliation, took him into his circle of closest friends and soon chose him as a general for the war.
settings.readers: Readers who know Celsus as one of Otho's generals (1:87) see how he came to be one, and Tacitus's remark that his loyalty to Otho was "as faultless as it was unlucky."

settings.what: The letters between Otho and Vitellius
settings.by: Otho, then Vitellius, then Fabius Valens
settings.to: each other, and the Praetorian and city cohorts
settings.when: early in Otho's reign, between January and March 69
settings.why: To bargain for peace with offers of money and quiet retirement, and to sound the troops in each other's camps. Neither side gave way; the letters ended in insults (1:74).
settings.readers: Readers know neither letter-writer kept the peace. Tacitus calls the offers "foolish and undignified pretending on both sides" (1:74).

settings.what: The edict praising Cluvius Rufus
settings.by: the author of an edict, whom Tacitus does not name
settings.to: the public
settings.when: as news came in from the provinces, shortly before it was learned that Spain had turned to Vitellius
settings.why: To honor Spain's governor for its oath to Otho. Tacitus says that right away it was learned that Spain had turned to Vitellius, so the praise was out of date as soon as it was published.
settings.readers: Readers who know Cluvius Rufus as a governor and a skilled speaker (1:8) see his praise overtaken by events within the same verse.

settings.what: Otho's speech after the night riot
settings.by: Otho
settings.to: the soldiers in the Praetorian camp
settings.when: after the night riot (1:80-82) and before Otho left Rome on 14 March (1:90); Tacitus gives no date for the riot
settings.why: To quiet the soldiers who had burst into his dinner, to teach that an army lives by obedience, to defend the Senate, and to name only two men for punishment. It ended with 5,000 sesterces for each soldier, paid before he spoke (1:82).
settings.readers: Readers see Otho defend the Senate against his own Guard. Tacitus calls the speech one "meant to rebuke and soothe" (1:85).
views: Tacitus's judgment
The speech was "meant to rebuke and soothe" (1:85).
Luke 7:8
The centurion's words describe command by the same chain Otho names.

settings.what: The Senate's debate and vote against Vitellius
settings.by: the senators, speaking in turn
settings.to: one another and Otho, in the Senate House
settings.when: after Otho's speech to the soldiers (1:83-84)
settings.why: To declare Vitellius "an enemy and a traitor to his country" at a time when silence looked defiant and frankness looked suspicious. Tacitus says the cautious stuck to common insults, some threw out true accusations only amid shouting, and others drowned themselves out in a jumble of words.
settings.readers: The senators among Tacitus's readers knew that room. He tells them it was hard to keep "a safe balance in everything," which is a picture of what speech in the Senate was like in 69.

settings.what: Otho's farewell to the people
settings.by: Otho, in an assembly (and the crowd's shouts)
settings.to: the people of Rome
settings.when: 14 March 69, the day he left Rome
settings.why: To hold up the greatness of the city and the agreement of people and Senate, to speak moderately of Vitellius's party and to blame the legions' ignorance. Tacitus raises the question whether the speech was Otho's or his speechwriter's.
settings.readers: Readers are told that the speech may be a speechwriter's work and that the crowd's shouts came "from a sheer love of servitude." The book closes on flattery as it opened on it (1:1).
